Do you know Caroline?
Yes, she and Pierre run the general store. They keep the shelves stocked and the door open, which is more than a good many towns manage.
You talk to her much?
Only a greeting across the counter on Thursdays. That is the whole of our acquaintance, and it is a pleasant one.

Who runs this place?
Gunther, the curator. The library and the museum are both his, and he lets a cold writer sit in the warm for as long as I like.
Generous of him.
Enormously. I spend most of fall and winter under his roof and have never once been asked to justify myself.

There were children in here earlier.
Penny reads with them here most days. Pam's daughter, and a genuine lover of books, which places her in a small and excellent club in this valley.
You approve.
Wholeheartedly, and from the next table along.
You could say hello.
I would hate to interrupt a story. My admiration stays where it belongs, quietly on my side of the room.

Is the mayor any good?
I think so; the town runs and the festivals happen. I only see Lewis presiding at them, with a short speech and a great air of ceremony.
That is all you have got?
That is all. I see him the way the whole square does, fondly and from a distance.

Who is that at the bar?
Pam. She drives the bus, and in the evenings she is a fixture of this room, which I say with no judgment whatever, since so am I.
Fair point.
We nod. That is the extent of it, and it is a companionable sort of nod.

What is Shane's deal?
I do not know him. He works at Joja, from what the town says, and I see him in here most evenings; past that I would only be guessing.
Go on, guess.
I would rather not; I would only be inventing a man. He has never once asked me to explain myself either.

Emily never stops moving.
True, she serves half this room of an evening and still finds a word for everybody in it. That is a talent I would not have the stamina for.
You should tell her that.
I tip, and I thank her at the door. That is a writer's way of saying a thing without risking the sentence.

Have you met the woman with the ranch?
Only in passing; that is Marnie, with the ranch here in the forest. I see her in town and at the festivals, and that is the whole of my report.
Not much of a report.
The honest ones rarely are. I could invent you a better one, though you would catch me at it before the second sentence.

Who built half these houses?
Robin, the carpenter, from her shop up the mountain. The town is largely her handiwork. My cabin predates her mercy, and you can tell at a glance.
You should hire her.
I could never afford her, @. I buy my ink in installments as it is.

Do you know the scientist?
Only by name: Demetrius, from the house up the mountain. I have seen him at festivals.
Never spoken?
A greeting in passing, once or twice. I could not tell you anything about his work.

Maru builds robots, apparently.
So the town says, and I believe it without understanding a syllable of it. She is the inventor of that mountain household, and whatever she is making up there is well beyond my vocabulary.
You could ask her about it.
I could, though she would discover the full depth of my ignorance within a minute. I shall admire from the square, where the light is kinder to me.

context: fall, clear evening, Pelican Town, 4 hearts

The man in the black hoodie never says anything.
That is Sebastian, I believe, the quiet son of the mountain house. We have exchanged perhaps four words all told and I did not mind a single one of them.
You do not find that rude?
Good heavens, no. A man is entitled to his own quiet, and I have borrowed a great deal more than my share of the town's.
I suppose so.
Keep showing interest in them and they will get comfortable around you. It worked on me, and I am a great deal harder work than he is.

The young ones are down here every summer.
They are. Sam and Alex and the rest of them, loud as gulls and twice as quick, all over the square and the sand the moment it turns warm.
Does it bother you?
Not in the least. A beach with young people shouting on it is a better beach, and it does my dialogue a great deal of good.

Abigail was giving me a look just now.
I do not know what the look meant; that is Abigail, Pierre and Caroline's daughter. I see her about the square rather more often than behind this counter.
Do you know her at all?
To greet, and no further. The young people of this town have their own weather, and I would not presume to forecast it.

Haley was down here with her camera.
Was she? The morning light is good for it. We have only ever traded greetings, though I confess I would like to see her photographs.
You should ask her.
One day, when I have something to trade for it. A man with an unfinished novel has poor standing to ask anybody about their work.

context: winter, clear afternoon, Pelican Town, 5 hearts

Vincent nearly ran me over out there.
I am sorry to hear it; that is Jodi's boy, and he and Jas do run everywhere. Between the two of them they make more noise than the gulls, which I consider a public service.
The families here keep to themselves.
Mostly, I think. They are kind and they are busy, as families are.
Kent barely leaves the house.
I do not know about that. He was away at the war a long stretch, as the whole town knows, and I am glad he is home.

That old couple in town always wave at me.
George and Evelyn. She tends the gardens around the square, and those flowers are the only reason my spring walks can pass for research.
He does not seem as friendly.
He waves from his chair, which at my distance amounts to the same thing. I have never had cause to ask more of either of them.
